title: Sonar-TS: Search-Then-Verify Querying for Time Series
one_liner: Sonar-TS finds events in massive time-series databases by first narrowing down candidate windows with SQL, then verifying them with custom Python code.
lead: When you have years of stock prices, sensor readings, or heartbeat records and want to ask natural questions in plain English—like find all times when the price jumped suddenly or the pattern looked like a smooth climb—existing methods fail. They either drown in the huge amount of data or miss the actual shapes and patterns you are looking for. Sonar-TS is a hybrid method that uses database tricks to narrow the search space first, then validates with hand-built logic that understands the actual raw data.

problem.h2: Asking questions about patterns buried in time
paras: You have a database with millions of data points collected over weeks or years—stock prices ticking every second, factory sensors recording every minute, hospital monitors logging every heartbeat. You want to ask natural questions: when did the price spike? Find all times the curve looked smooth. Which periods had unusual jumps? The challenge is that the database is too big to read all at once, and the patterns you care about are shapes and anomalies, not simple numerical ranges.

Text-to-SQL methods exist, but they translate English into database queries designed for structured tables with clean columns—they are blind to shapes, curves, and anomalies. Time-series models can spot patterns but choke on ultra-long histories (years of data). Neither world talks to the other.

callout.html: How do you ask a natural-language question about patterns in massive, continuous time-series data when SQL sees only rows and columns, and machine learning models cannot handle the sheer length of history?

steps.text: Parse the English query and decide what properties to search for in the database.
Query the time-series database using a feature index to find candidate time windows meeting basic criteria.
Write custom Python code that checks the actual raw values in each candidate window against the full pattern request.
Execute the generated code on only the narrow set of candidates, not the entire dataset.
Report time intervals where both SQL and Python checks pass, eliminating false positives.

paras: The paper builds a two-stage pipeline: SQL finds rough candidates by querying abstract properties (ranges, counts, simple statistics), then Python verifies by reading the actual raw time values and testing the full pattern. Instead of one model trying to do everything, the paper splits the load between database logic and verification code.

hidden.h2: The hidden quantity: search recall vs verification cost
hidden.name: search recall and verification cost
paras: The key trade-off the paper balances is this: the SQL search must be broad enough to include all true answers (high recall), but narrow enough that the Python verifier does not waste time checking millions of false candidates. If the SQL is too strict, true answers are discarded before verification. If the SQL is too loose, verification drowns in noise.

The paper measures this trade-off by tuning how broad the SQL search is—relaxing it to catch more candidates at the cost of more verification work, or tightening it to verify faster but risk missing answers. The feature index (a pre-computed summary of ranges, counts, and simple properties per time window) lets the SQL search work without scanning all raw data.

heat.caption: Darker means more balance between catching real answers and avoiding wasted verification.

reads.html: The search part finds candidates fast but imprecisely. The verify part is precise but expensive. The paper tunes how strict the search is so the total cost stays low while the answer is not lost.

The feature index supports efficient SQL queries over continuous-valued time series. The generated Python verifier narrows candidate sets by executing detailed checks on raw signal data, trading verification cost for recall preservation.

mechanism.h2: Why it works: two minds, one question
paras: SQL databases are fast at filtering by simple rules: show me all times when a column was between 10 and 20, or where the average in a window fell. But SQL cannot describe a curve, an anomaly, or a smooth transition—it sees only numbers and ranges. Machine learning models understand curves and shapes but cannot efficiently scan billions of rows.

Sonar-TS solves this by having SQL do the heavy filtering (throwing away 99% of the data) using a fast feature index—a pre-built summary of simple properties per candidate window. Then, on only the narrow survivor set, it runs generated Python code that reads the actual raw values and tests the full pattern. This is like sonar: first, send a broad ping to narrow the search space (SQL search), then lock onto the target with precise verification (Python code). The pipeline works because filtering first is cheap (SQL is optimized for it) and verification second is affordable (only a few candidates remain).

stages.s: Generate SQL query using the feature index
SQL returns candidate time windows (thousands, not billions)
Generate Python verifier code from the full pattern
Run verifier on only the candidates
Time intervals matching both SQL and Python checks

math.words: total_score = SQL_recall * verification_cost_ratio, where recall is the fraction of true answers the SQL finds, and cost_ratio is the number of candidates the Python must check divided by the total data points.
symbols: fraction of true answers caught by SQL search
number of time windows returned by SQL
all data points in the database

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose the database has 1,000,000 time points.
There are 100 true answers (windows matching the pattern).
SQL search returns 10,000 candidates (includes most true answers, plus false positives).
Recall from SQL: 95 out of 100 true answers found, so recall_SQL = 0.95.
Cost ratio: 10,000 / 1,000,000 = 0.01 (verifier touches 1% of the data).
If SQL were too strict and returned only 1,000 candidates, recall might drop to 0.70, giving quality = 0.70 * 0.999 = 0.699—lower overall because answers were lost.

math.note: The formula balances how many true answers the SQL finds against how much work the verifier must do.

items.b: Feature index does not match the query intent.
items.html: If the SQL search looks for low values but the pattern actually needs to detect a sudden jump, the SQL index returns the wrong candidates and Python cannot fix it. The search stage must be tuned for each query type.
If the verifier code misunderstands the pattern (e.g., tests for the wrong threshold or reads the wrong column), it filters out true answers. Code generation must be careful.
If the pattern spans longer than the model expects (e.g., a trend lasting 30 days when the verifier was written for 3 days), verification fails silently and returns incomplete results.
Tune the SQL search to be generous (accept candidates that look plausible), generate Python verifiers that carefully test the full pattern, and validate on known examples before running live queries.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small time-series database (e.g., 100,000 data points from a sine wave with noise and occasional jumps). Write a natural-language query like find all times when the signal jumped up then down in under 5 minutes. Create a feature index by summarizing the data into candidate windows. Generate SQL that finds windows where the maximum and minimum are far apart. Generate Python that verifies the exact jump timing. Measure: of the true jumps inserted into the data, how many did the pipeline find (recall)? How much faster was the search than scanning all data (speedup)? The search is faster because SQL filters out most candidates using pre-computed summaries, and only the small survivor set requires Python verification—avoiding full data scans.
demo.closing: The demo must show that Sonar-TS finds real patterns fast, not by luck, but because SQL screening actually worked and Python verification actually checked.
